column2: Back

Reads the passwd account database through the system’s configured lookup services; results can include local and centrally managed accounts. It does not reveal password hashes.
getent: Get entries from a configured system database.
passwd database: Account records containing names, user numbers, home folders and login programs.

On Debian, interactively creates a user and normally a home folder. Supply a username, for example adduser jordan; administrator privileges are usually required. The source is a command template.
User account: An identity used to sign in and own files.
Home folder: A user’s personal directory.

Template: usermod -aG GROUP USER. -G selects supplementary groups; -a appends them without removing existing memberships. New membership normally takes effect in a new login session.
Supplementary group: An extra group that grants shared access or permissions.

column1:
id user
Show a user’s identity and groups.
column2:
Shows the user number, primary group and supplementary groups for the account named user. Replace user with the intended account name.
UID: User identifier, the number representing an account.
GID: Group identifier, the number representing a group.

column1:
ssh-keygen -t -a -f -C
Create a login key with chosen settings.
column2:
Incomplete option template: -t needs a key type, -a a number of passphrase-protection rounds, -f an output filename and -C a comment. Example: ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -a 100 -f ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 -C "admin key". Keep the private key secret.
SSH: Secure Shell, encrypted remote access.
Key pair: A public key you share and a private key you keep secret.
Passphrase: A password protecting the saved private key.
Ed25519: A type of public-key cryptography.

Copies a public key to a remote account’s authorized_keys file. Supply a destination such as user@host; -i can select the public-key file. You need an existing way to authenticate.
Public key: The shareable half of a login key pair.
authorized_keys: The remote account’s list of public keys allowed to log in.
Authenticate: Prove who you are.

column1:
ssh -i -o
Connect using a chosen key and settings.
column2:
Incomplete template: -i needs a private-key filename, -o needs an option=value setting, and a destination is required. Example: ssh -i ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 -o IdentitiesOnly=yes user@host.
SSH: Secure Shell, encrypted remote access.
Private key: The secret half of a login key pair.
IdentitiesOnly=yes: Restrict offered login identities to those configured explicitly.

Validates your sudo credentials without running another command. It may ask for your password and refreshes the cached authorization timestamp when policy allows.
sudo: Run authorized actions as another user, usually the administrator.
Credentials: Information used to prove your identity.

Queries the Debian package database. -W uses show format, normally printing package names and versions; listed records are not necessarily all currently installed.
Package: A managed bundle of software files.
Debian: A Linux operating-system family used by Proxmox.

Installs sudo and any required supporting packages on Debian-based systems. Requires administrator privileges, such as an existing root session.
APT: Advanced Package Tool, Debian’s software management tools.
Package: A managed software bundle.
sudo: A tool for authorized actions as another user.
Root: The system’s administrator account.

Opens the current user’s SSH client configuration in nano. Add per-host connection settings here; this is different from the server’s sshd_config file.
nano: A terminal text editor.
~: Your home folder.
SSH client: The program that starts a secure remote connection.
Configuration: Saved program settings.

Incomplete Bash template: supply an entry number, for example history -d 123. Removes it from the current history list; saved history may also need updating. It does not erase other logs or guarantee secret removal.
Bash: A command interpreter used in many Linux terminals.
Shell history: A record of previously entered commands.

Checks the SSH server configuration and host-key sanity without starting the server. Successful checks normally produce no output; inspect echo $? immediately afterward for the exit status.
sshd: The Secure Shell server program.
Host key: A key used to identify a server.
Exit status: A number indicating a command’s result; zero usually means success.

A pipeline fragment, not a standalone command: put a command before |. grep searches its output; -E enables extended patterns and -i ignores letter case. The pattern ^ matches the start of every line, so this exact pattern does not narrow the output.
Pipe (|): Pass one command’s output into another.
Regular expression: A pattern for matching text.
^: A pattern marker for the start of a line.

Prints the exit status of the most recently completed command or pipeline. Check it immediately: another command replaces it. Zero usually means success; other values depend on the program.
Exit status: A numeric result returned by a command.
Shell: The program that interprets commands.
$?: A shell variable holding the last exit status.

-l shows permissions, ownership, size and modification time; -a also includes names beginning with a dot, including . and ... Lists the current directory unless a path is supplied.
Permissions: Rules controlling who can read, change or run a file.
Directory: A folder.
Dotfile: A file whose name starts with a dot, usually hidden in ordinary listings.

column1:
sudo mv
Move or rename files as administrator.
column2:
Incomplete template: supply a source and destination, for example sudo mv old.conf new.conf. Moving can overwrite a destination file; check paths first.
sudo: Run an authorized command as another user, usually root.
mv: Move or rename files and directories.
Path: A file or folder’s location.

column1:
sudo systemctl reload ssh
Reload the SSH service’s settings.
column2:
As administrator, asks the systemd service named ssh to reload its settings without a full service restart. Check configuration with sshd -t first. The service must support reload; its name varies by system.
sudo: Run an authorized command as another user.
systemd: Linux’s system and service manager.
SSH: Secure Shell, encrypted remote access.
Reload: Ask a running service to reread its settings.

column1:
sudo cp -a
Copy files while preserving their details.
column2:
Incomplete template: supply source and destination. -a copies directories recursively and preserves links, permissions, ownership and timestamps where possible. Administrator privileges can allow preservation of ownership.
sudo: Run an authorized command as another user.
Archive mode (-a): Copy a directory tree while preserving file properties.
Symbolic link: A file that points to another path.
Recursive: Include everything inside nested folders.

column1:
sudo systemctl reload
Reload a chosen service’s settings.
column2:
Incomplete template: supply a service name, for example sudo systemctl reload ssh. Requests a reload from a running service that supports it. This differs from daemon-reload, which rereads systemd unit definitions.
sudo: Run an authorized command as another user.
systemd: Linux’s system and service manager.
Service: A background program.
Unit definition: Settings describing a resource managed by systemd.

column1:
chmod 600
Allow only the owner to read and write.
column2:
Incomplete template: supply a file path, for example chmod 600 ~/.ssh/id_ed25519. Sets owner permissions to read and write, and removes group and other permissions. It does not change ownership.
chmod: Change access permissions.
600: Owner read (4) plus write (2); group and others get no access.
Owner: The account that owns a file.

Starts the target user’s login shell. -u selects username; -i requests a login environment and normally changes to that user’s home folder. Replace username with the intended account; type exit to leave.
sudo: Run authorized actions as another user.
Login shell: A command session initialized like a fresh login.
Environment: Settings passed to running programs.

Shows the Proxmox version plus installed component and package versions. -v requests verbose output.
Proxmox VE: Proxmox Virtual Environment, a platform for running virtual machines and containers.
Package: A managed bundle of software.
Verbose: More detailed output.

Shows the current time, time since startup, logged-in user count and load averages for 1, 5 and 15 minutes. Load averages measure runnable tasks and tasks in uninterruptible waits; they are not CPU percentages.
Load average: Average number of tasks running, ready to run or in certain waiting states.
CPU: Central Processing Unit, the processor that executes instructions.

With no subcommand, defaults to list-units: shows units currently in memory, normally active, pending or failed. It does not list every installed unit file.
systemd: Linux’s system and service manager.
Unit: A managed resource, such as a service, device or mounted filesystem.

-o selects columns: device name, size, device type, filesystem type and mount locations. Displays the storage hierarchy. Device names can change between restarts.
Block device: Storage accessed in fixed-size pieces, such as a disk.
Filesystem: The structure that organizes files on storage.
Mount point: A folder where a filesystem becomes accessible.

-a includes internal and hidden logical volumes. -o selects volume name, group, size, segment type, data usage and metadata usage. Monitor both percentage columns for thin pools; some fields are blank when not applicable.
LVM: Logical Volume Manager, a tool for organizing disk space into flexible volumes.
Logical volume: A virtual storage device created by LVM.
Volume group: A pool of storage used to create logical volumes.
Segment type: How a portion of a logical volume stores its data.
Thin pool: Shared storage allocated to volumes as data is written.
Metadata: Information tracking where stored data belongs.

Reports total, used and available filesystem space. -h prints readable sizes using powers of 1024. This does not measure free capacity inside an LVM thin pool.
Filesystem: The structure organizing files on storage.
Mounted: Attached to a folder so files can be accessed.
LVM thin pool: Shared storage that allocates space to virtual volumes as needed.

column1:
ip -br link
Show network interfaces and their states briefly.
column2:
-br requests brief output; link shows interfaces, their state, hardware addresses and link flags. This checks interfaces rather than assigned IP addresses.
Network interface: A physical or virtual connection used for network traffic.
Hardware address: A link-layer identifier, often a MAC address.
MAC: Media Access Control, the address used to identify an Ethernet interface.

-br requests brief output; addr lists interfaces, their states and assigned IP addresses, including address-prefix lengths.
IP: Internet Protocol, the system for addressing and routing network traffic.
Network interface: A physical or virtual network connection.
Prefix length: The number of address bits identifying the network, such as /24.

Prints the network configuration file used by ifupdown-style tools on this host. Saved settings may differ from the currently running network; included files can hold additional configuration.
cat: Print a file’s contents.
ifupdown: Tools that activate and deactivate network interfaces using saved settings.
Network interface: A physical or virtual network connection.
Configuration: Saved settings.

column1:
bridge vlan show
Show bridge VLAN membership and tagging.
column2:
Lists VLAN settings on Linux bridge ports. PVID marks the VLAN assigned to incoming untagged traffic; Egress Untagged means outgoing traffic for that VLAN leaves without a tag.
Bridge: A software switch connecting network interfaces.
VLAN: Virtual Local Area Network, a logical separation within an Ethernet network.
PVID: Port VLAN Identifier, the default VLAN for incoming untagged frames.
Egress: Traffic leaving a port.
Tag: A label in a network frame identifying its VLAN.

Lists interface entries exposed by the running kernel, including physical and virtual interfaces. A saved interface configuration alone does not make an interface appear here.
sysfs: A virtual filesystem exposing kernel and device information.
Kernel: The operating system’s core that manages hardware and resources.
Network interface: A connection used to send and receive network traffic.

column1:
lspci | grep -i ethernet
Find detected PCI Ethernet devices.
column2:
lspci lists PCI devices; the pipe sends that list to grep. -i searches for ethernet without regard to letter case. This does not list every network adapter, such as USB adapters.
PCI: Peripheral Component Interconnect, a family of hardware connections for devices.
Ethernet: A common wired networking technology.
Pipe (|): Send one command’s output to another.
grep: A program for finding matching text.
USB: Universal Serial Bus, a common external device connection.

Lists virtual machines configured in Proxmox, including their identifiers, names and states. It does not list LXC containers.
Proxmox VE: Proxmox Virtual Environment, a virtualization platform.
Virtual machine: A software-defined computer with its own operating system.
QEMU: Software that provides virtual computer hardware.
KVM: Kernel-based Virtual Machine, Linux support for hardware-assisted virtualization.

Lists LXC containers configured in Proxmox, including identifiers, states and names.
Proxmox VE: Proxmox Virtual Environment, a virtualization platform.
LXC: Linux Containers, isolated Linux environments sharing the host’s kernel.
Kernel: The core of an operating system.
Host: The computer running virtual machines or containers.

Starts an encrypted remote session to 192.168.178.10 using the root account. Login succeeds only if the server permits that account and accepts your authentication.
SSH: Secure Shell, encrypted remote access.
Root: The Linux administrator account.
IP address: A numeric network address identifying a destination.
Authentication: Proving your identity.

Ends the current shell; in an SSH shell this normally closes that remote session. In a nested shell it returns you to the previous shell.
Shell: A program that interprets typed commands.
SSH: Secure Shell, encrypted remote access.

Runs free -h repeatedly, refreshing the display every 2 seconds. -n sets the interval and -h makes memory sizes readable. Press Ctrl+C to stop.
RAM: Random Access Memory, the working memory used by programs.
Swap: Storage space that can hold memory pages outside RAM.
Available memory: An estimate of memory usable by new applications without swapping.

Runs free -h repeatedly, refreshing the display every 1 second. -n sets the interval and -h makes memory sizes readable. Press Ctrl+C to stop.
RAM: Random Access Memory, the working memory used by programs.
Swap: Storage space that can hold memory pages outside RAM.
Available memory: An estimate of memory usable by new applications without swapping.
